top_line: The US ended its 12-year military mission in Iraq, and Morocco named its first woman PM, while Iran-US tensions kept oil elevated. Anthropic's leaked IPO filing revealed huge losses and an AI 'existential risk' warning, and a new UPI merchant fee looms from October 15.
claude_take: Today's pattern is receding American commitments and rising Asian/AI-industry stakes: the US steps back from Iraq just as North Korea deepens its bet on Russia, and Anthropic's IPO shows how much capital — and risk — is now riding on AI. For India, the through-line is practical: watch your October 1 and October 15 money-rule changes.

top5.why: Ends the 12-year US military mission and reshapes Middle East security

sections.title: World
sections.gist: The US closed out its Iraq mission, Morocco made history with its first woman PM, and Iran, Russia and North Korea all raised the geopolitical temperature.

items.headline: US completes final troop withdrawal from Iraq
items.what: The US military said Wednesday it has pulled every remaining soldier out of Iraq, ending a 12-year mission that began to fight the Islamic State group. The last troops left a base in the Kurdish north. Iraq declared a two-day holiday, calling it 'Sovereignty Day.'
items.why_it_matters: It removes the biggest remaining US military footprint in the Middle East, and hands Iraq's security fully to a government with close ties to Iran.
items.context: The US invaded Iraq in 2003 and stayed on after 2014 to help fight ISIS, which once controlled a third of the country. Baghdad's government, closer to Iran, had pushed for a firm exit deadline.
items.next: Watch whether ISIS remnants regroup, and whether Iranian-backed militias fill the security gap the US leaves behind.
items.insight: The exit lands the same week Iran is stonewalling the US over Hormuz — a reminder Washington's regional leverage is shrinking on two fronts at once.

terms.meaning: The militant group that seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014, since mostly defeated.

items.headline: Morocco names its first-ever woman prime minister
items.what: King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Zahra Mansouri, a lawyer and Marrakesh's mayor, as prime minister on Tuesday. Her centre-right party won last week's election with 97 of 395 seats. She must now form a coalition government.
items.why_it_matters: It's a symbolic breakthrough for women's political representation in North Africa, though the king still holds final say over major decisions.
items.context: Morocco is a constitutional monarchy where the king holds real power but a prime minister runs day-to-day government. No woman has held the job since the post was created in 1955.
items.next: Mansouri now has weeks to negotiate a coalition and submit her cabinet list for the king's approval.

items.headline: Iran-US standoff over Hormuz drags on, oil rises
items.what: Iran is sticking to its terms for reopening the Strait of Hormuz — sanctions relief and unfrozen funds — after the US rejected its offer. Brent crude has traded above $100 a barrel for most of September on the uncertainty.
items.why_it_matters: Every extra week of standoff keeps oil, and so petrol and shipping costs, higher — a direct hit on India's import bill.
items.context: Hormuz is the narrow sea lane between Iran and Oman that carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Iran partly blockaded it earlier this year after US strikes on its nuclear sites, and wants the blockade traded for concessions.
items.next: Watch for any fresh diplomatic signal before oil markets price in a longer blockade.
items.insight: Iran's leverage here is weaker than in past standoffs — Gulf oil exports have already rebounded to 98% of pre-war levels, easing the pressure on Washington to cave.

terms.meaning: A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through.

items.headline: North Korea readies 10,000 more troops for Russia
items.what: Ukraine's President Zelenskyy said North Korea is preparing to send another 10,000 soldiers to fight for Russia, on top of more than 8,000 already there. Pyongyang has not confirmed the number. Moscow has reportedly helped North Korea build attack-drone factories in return.
items.why_it_matters: It shows Russia still can't generate enough of its own soldiers three years into the war, and deepens a Moscow-Pyongyang alliance that worries Seoul and Washington.
items.context: North Korea and Russia signed a mutual-defence pact in 2024. Since then, Pyongyang has sent thousands of troops to help Russia fight Ukraine, mainly around the Kursk region, in exchange for money, fuel and military technology.
items.next: Watch for confirmation from Pyongyang and whether Russia's new 15,500-troop mobilisation reduces its need for North Korean reinforcements.

items.headline: Putin orders fresh Russian army mobilisation
items.what: President Putin signed a decree adding 15,500 troops to Russia's armed forces, the fourth expansion this year, as war losses in Ukraine mount. The move comes as Kyiv warns Russia is also leaning more heavily on North Korean reinforcements.
items.why_it_matters: Four mobilisations in a year signal Russia's war machine is burning through manpower faster than it can quietly replace it.
items.context: Russia has relied on repeated partial mobilisations and high enlistment bonuses, rather than a single mass draft, to avoid the public backlash its 2022 mobilisation triggered.
items.next: Watch Ukraine's own manpower and Western-aid numbers as the war grinds into a fourth winter.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: J&K's assembly pushed for full statehood, a Delhi court kept two riots-case activists in custody, and UP's Rajya Sabha polls were notified.

items.headline: J&K Assembly demands full statehood be restored
items.what: Jammu & Kashmir's Assembly passed a resolution urging the central government to immediately restore full statehood, with 60 of 90 MLAs backing it. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah moved the motion; the BJP walked out in protest.
items.why_it_matters: The resolution is symbolic — the Centre alone can restore statehood — but it keeps pressure on Delhi ahead of national attention on J&K.
items.context: J&K lost statehood in 2019 when the government revoked its special status and split it into two union territories. It got an elected assembly back in 2024, but Delhi still runs security and land.
items.next: No timeline from the central government yet; watch whether it features in the next Parliament session.

items.headline: Delhi court again refuses bail in 2020 riots case
items.what: The Delhi High Court denied bail, for a third time, to activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the case over 2020's Delhi riots. Judges said they could not soften bail terms the Supreme Court had already set in January.
items.why_it_matters: It keeps two prominent activists in custody for a sixth year without a verdict, reviving debate over how UAPA is used against government critics.
items.context: Khalid and Imam have been jailed without trial since 2020 under UAPA, a strict anti-terror law, accused of conspiring in riots that killed 53 people in northeast Delhi. Both deny the charges.
items.next: The Supreme Court said bail could be revisited after a year or once protected witnesses are examined.

terms.meaning: The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act — a strict law that makes it hard to get bail in terror-related cases.

items.headline: Election Commission notifies Rajya Sabha polls for UP
items.what: The Election Commission notified elections for 10 Rajya Sabha seats and 11 state legislative council seats from Uttar Pradesh. Nominations close October 6, and voting is set for October 16.
items.why_it_matters: These seats shift the balance of India's upper house, which can block or slow bills the ruling party passes in the Lok Sabha.
items.context: Rajya Sabha members, unlike the directly-elected Lok Sabha, are chosen by state legislators. Parties are already naming candidates — the Samajwadi Party picked Ramgopal Yadav among its nominees.
items.next: Watch candidate lists from the BJP and opposition over the next week.

sections.title: Affects you
sections.gist: October brings a wave of money-rule changes — UPI fees, SBI ATM limits, LPG biometric checks — plus tighter Delhi pollution rules.

items.headline: New UPI fee on shop payments over ₹2,000 from Oct 15
items.what: From October 15, shops will pay a 0.4% fee, capped at ₹300, on UPI payments they receive above ₹2,000. That's up to ₹8 on a ₹2,000 bill. Payments between friends and family, and to small merchants, stay free.
items.why_it_matters: Shops may pass the cost on with a surcharge or nudge you toward cash for bigger bills.
items.context: UPI — the tap-to-pay system behind PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm — has been free since 2016 to push people off cash. Banks say running it costs money and want a cut.
items.next: Fuel, rail and telecom payments get a flat ₹5 fee instead of the 0.4% rate.
items.insight: The fee lands on shops, not shoppers — but expect informal surcharges to creep in anyway, especially at small kirana stores with thin margins.

terms.meaning: Merchant Discount Rate — the small cut a shop pays on each digital payment it accepts.

items.headline: SBI cuts free ATM withdrawals for salary accounts
items.what: From October 1, SBI salary-account holders get only 5 free transactions a month at other banks' ATMs, down from 10. Beyond that, it's ₹23 plus GST per withdrawal and ₹11 plus GST for balance checks and the like.
items.why_it_matters: If you regularly withdraw cash at other banks' ATMs, track your count — extra withdrawals now cost real money.
items.context: Banks earn less on cheap salary accounts, so they're trimming perks like unlimited free ATM use to cut costs as digital payments eat into their fee income.
items.next: Check your bank's app for your exact free-transaction count before month-end.

items.headline: LPG subsidy now needs Aadhaar fingerprint or face scan
items.what: From October 1, domestic LPG customers must complete Aadhaar biometric authentication — a fingerprint or face scan — to keep booking subsidised cylinders at the regular price. Those who skip it may be charged the full, unsubsidised rate.
items.why_it_matters: Households that don't verify in time could suddenly pay market price for their next cylinder refill.
items.context: The government has pushed Aadhaar checks across welfare schemes for years to weed out duplicate or fake accounts receiving subsidies meant for one household.
items.next: Verify at your gas agency or via the distributor's app before your next booking.

items.headline: Delhi tightens winter pollution rules, doubles some fines
items.what: Delhi-NCR's air-quality panel tightened its winter action plan: diesel-generator and inter-city bus curbs now start a stage earlier, and penalties for generator violations double from the very first stage instead of the second.
items.why_it_matters: If you own a diesel generator, an old truck, or run a construction site in Delhi-NCR, curbs now bite sooner and cost more.
items.context: GRAP is the graded response Delhi triggers as air quality worsens each winter, adding restrictions in four stages. Old vehicles and construction are usually the first targets.
items.next: GRAP stages activate automatically as Delhi's air quality index crosses set thresholds this winter.

terms.meaning: Graded Response Action Plan — Delhi's staged pollution-control rules that tighten as air quality worsens.

items.headline: Supreme Court rules out total Diwali firecracker ban
items.what: The Supreme Court said it won't impose a blanket firecracker ban in Delhi-NCR this Diwali, nor allow unrestricted bursting — instead favouring fixed hours. It may also permit joint 'laris' crackers under conditions, pending a report on barium-based crackers by October 15.
items.why_it_matters: Families planning Diwali celebrations will get clearer, time-bound rules rather than a shifting patchwork of local bans.
items.context: Delhi's air quality turns hazardous most winters, and firecrackers are one of several contributing sources alongside vehicles, construction dust and stubble burning from neighbouring states.
items.next: The court will decide which cracker types to allow after reviewing the CPCB's report on October 15.

items.headline: EPF wage ceiling rise takes full effect this month
items.what: October is the first full month under the government's higher EPF wage ceiling — raised from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 from September 17. More of a salaried employee's pay now falls under mandatory provident-fund contributions.
items.why_it_matters: More employees now have a bigger slice of pay locked into retirement savings — lower take-home pay now, more savings later.
items.context: EPF is India's mandatory retirement-savings scheme for salaried workers, funded by a matching cut from both employee and employer pay, capped at a set wage level.
items.next: Check your October payslip to see the new deduction reflected.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: Oil stayed elevated on the Hormuz standoff, Wall Street and Indian markets slipped on high bond yields, and Anthropic's leaked IPO filing stunned investors.

items.headline: Oil stays elevated as Iran-US standoff drags on
items.what: Brent crude has traded above $100 a barrel most of September and topped $108 at one point this week, as Iran and the US remain deadlocked over reopening the Strait of Hormuz. WTI crude sits near $89.
items.why_it_matters: Higher oil raises India's import bill and keeps pressure on the rupee and on inflation.
items.context: Brent and WTI are the two global oil-price benchmarks. Elevated prices ripple into fuel, transport and manufacturing costs worldwide, including in India, which imports most of its crude.
items.next: Any Hormuz breakthrough, or fresh escalation, would move oil sharply either way.

items.headline: Wall Street mixed as bond yields hit decade highs
items.what: The Dow fell 0.3% and the Nasdaq slipped 0.1% on Tuesday as the 30-year Treasury yield crossed 5.6%, its highest since 2002, and the 10-year hit a 2007-level high near 5.3%. Investors are awaiting a key US inflation report.
items.why_it_matters: Higher US borrowing costs tend to pull money out of emerging markets like India's, adding pressure on the rupee.
items.context: Treasury yields are the interest rate the US government pays to borrow. When they rise, borrowing gets pricier everywhere, and investors often shift money out of stocks and into bonds.
items.next: This week's US inflation data (core PCE) could push yields — and stock moves — further.
items.insight: The 30-year yield at a 24-year high, even as the Fed has been cutting short-term rates, signals markets are betting on persistently high government borrowing and inflation, not a slowdown.

terms.meaning: The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, stripping out volatile food and energy prices.

items.headline: Sensex, Nifty fall for a third straight session
items.what: The Sensex closed down 48.78 points at 72,480.29, and the Nifty fell 95.75 points to 22,620.45. It's the third losing session in a row, as rebounding oil prices and a weak rupee weigh on sentiment.
items.why_it_matters: A weaker rupee makes imports — including oil — costlier, which can feed into prices you pay.
items.context: Sensex and Nifty are India's two main stock benchmarks, tracking the BSE's 30 and NSE's 50 largest listed companies. The rupee traded near ₹96 to the dollar, close to record lows.
items.next: Watch Friday's US inflation data and any Hormuz news for the next directional cue.

items.headline: Gold near $4,180; Bitcoin holds September gains near $83K
items.what: Gold traded around $4,177 an ounce, and Bitcoin held near $83,500, both still well off their 2026 record highs but up for the month. Spot Bitcoin ETFs saw just $31 million of inflows Monday, down sharply from the prior session.
items.why_it_matters: Gold near record levels reflects investors hedging against inflation and geopolitical risk; crypto's cooling ETF inflows suggest that rally is losing steam.
items.context: Gold hit an all-time high above $5,589 an ounce in January and has cooled since. Bitcoin is trying to climb back toward the multi-month high it hit last week, holding on to its September gains.
items.next: $82K–$83K is bitcoin's near-term support; a break below could accelerate selling.

items.headline: Anthropic's leaked IPO filing shows $42 billion loss
items.what: A leaked prospectus shows Anthropic, the maker of Claude, lost nearly $42 billion in 2025 even as revenue jumped over 1,000% to $4.6 billion. The company has committed $518 billion to computing power over the next decade and hopes to list in November at a $2 trillion-plus valuation.
items.why_it_matters: It would be one of the biggest tech IPOs ever, and a real-world test of whether investors will fund AI's enormous, unprofitable compute bills.
items.context: An IPO prospectus is the detailed disclosure document a company files before selling shares to the public, listing its finances and risks. Anthropic's filing also warned its own AI models could pose 'catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.'
items.next: Anthropic is targeting a November listing; watch for the official prospectus and set price range.
items.insight: Nearly half of Anthropic's revenue flows through just two cloud partners, Amazon and Google — a concentration risk that gives both firms outsized leverage over an AI 'competitor' they also fund.

items.headline: RBI's rate call looms as economists split on a hike
items.what: The Reserve Bank of India's rate-setting panel meets October 5-7, with economists divided on whether it raises rates by 0.25 percentage points to fight inflation from high oil prices, or holds steady at 5.25% for more data.
items.why_it_matters: A hike would make home and car loans pricier almost immediately, but could help tame inflation from costly oil.
items.context: The repo rate is what the RBI charges banks for short-term loans, and it filters through to loan and deposit rates across the economy. It's been flat at 5.25% since August.
items.next: The RBI's decision lands October 7 — watch for its tone on oil-driven inflation.

terms.meaning: The interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to banks — it steers loan rates economy-wide.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: Top AI companies signed a voluntary safety accord with Trump, OpenAI slashed API prices, and Claude arrived on AWS servers inside India.

items.headline: Top AI CEOs sign Trump-brokered 'self-police' accord
items.what: Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Google's Sundar Pichai, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and xAI's Elon Musk joined President Trump in signing a voluntary accord for AI companies to run internal and outside safety reviews. Trump called it 'morally binding.'
items.why_it_matters: With no binding AI law from Congress, this self-policing pact is currently the closest thing the US has to AI safety oversight.
items.context: It's a voluntary pledge, not a law — each company sets up a board committee to review an independent auditor's findings on whether its internal safety controls actually work.
items.next: Watch whether the promised external auditors and board committees are named, and whether any company breaches the pact without consequence.
items.insight: 'Voluntary' and 'morally binding' aren't enforceable — the accord has no penalties, so its real test is whether firms keep to it once AI competition intensifies.

items.headline: AWS brings Claude AI models to India, Seoul, Singapore
items.what: Amazon Web Services expanded access to Anthropic's Claude models — Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5 — with local data processing in India, and in-region hosting in Seoul and Singapore, on its Bedrock cloud platform.
items.why_it_matters: It makes it easier for Indian banks, hospitals and government bodies to adopt AI tools built on Claude while meeting data-residency rules.
items.context: Companies handling sensitive data — banks, hospitals, government bodies — often must legally keep that data inside national borders, which this kind of local AI hosting makes possible.
items.next: Watch for Indian enterprise and government AI deployments to pick up as data-residency concerns ease.

items.headline: OpenAI halves API prices for its newest GPT-6 models
items.what: OpenAI cut prices for its GPT-6 Sol and Luna models to half or less of what developers paid for the previous version, crediting better caching and inference. Sol now costs $2 per million input tokens, down from $4.
items.why_it_matters: Cheaper AI compute lets more startups and businesses afford to build AI features, intensifying competition across the industry.
items.context: AI companies charge developers per 'token' — a chunk of text — to use their models through code. Falling prices make it cheaper for apps and businesses to build on AI.
items.next: Watch rival labs, including Anthropic and Google, for matching price cuts.

items.headline: China plans AI-made geological map of Mars by 2028
items.what: China announced plans to use artificial intelligence to build the world's first fully AI-generated geological map of Mars, targeting completion by the end of 2028, drawing on data from its Mars missions and orbiters.
items.why_it_matters: It shows AI increasingly automating scientific work once done by hand, potentially speeding up site-selection for future Mars missions.
items.context: Mapping a planet's geology — its rock types, fault lines and surface features — normally takes scientists years of manual analysis of satellite and rover images.
items.next: Watch for China to share methodology or early results as the project progresses.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: New research traced bats and Alzheimer's-linked immune damage to unexpected origins, while Antarctic ice and Mars exploration both made headlines.

items.headline: WHO issues guidance to prevent heat deaths at events
items.what: The World Health Organization published new guidance for preventing heat-related illness at mass gatherings, saying most cases can be prevented or treated on-site with timely risk management. It follows a string of heat-linked incidents at large events worldwide in recent years.
items.why_it_matters: Organisers of large events, including in India, now have a clearer on-site playbook to prevent heat deaths as summers get hotter.
items.context: Concerts, festivals, pilgrimages and sports events increasingly draw huge crowds in extreme heat, and rising global temperatures make heatstroke and dehydration a growing risk at such gatherings.
items.next: Watch whether event organisers and local governments adopt the WHO's guidance ahead of the next hot season.

items.headline: Study: bats may have first evolved in Europe
items.what: A worldwide study of 103 bat genomes and 44 fossils found bats almost certainly originated in Europe about 65 million years ago, not in Africa or Asia as long assumed. The 137-scientist Bat1K team put the odds of a European origin at over 99%.
items.why_it_matters: It rewrites a basic fact of mammal evolution and shows how combining genetics with fossils can resolve decades-old debates.
items.context: Bats are the only mammals with powered flight, but their fragile, thin bones rarely fossilise well, so scientists have long struggled to pin down where they first appeared.
items.next: Expect follow-up work on which early bat lineages first left Europe, and when echolocation evolved.

items.headline: Alzheimer's-driving immune cells may start outside the brain
items.what: Researchers found that in mice, immune cells called T cells get 'switched on' by dendritic cells in lymph nodes — far from the brain — before travelling in and damaging neurons. Removing those lymph-node dendritic cells cut brain damage and preserved memory.
items.why_it_matters: It suggests future Alzheimer's drugs could work by calming the immune system outside the brain, which may be easier to reach safely than the brain itself.
items.context: Lymph nodes are small immune-system stations spread through the body. Scientists still don't know exactly what triggers them to activate these brain-damaging T cells in the first place.
items.next: Watch for attempts to replicate this pathway in human tissue or early clinical trials.
items.insight: Most Alzheimer's drugs target plaques directly inside the brain, a hard and risky place to intervene — this points to an outside-in approach that could sidestep that problem.

items.headline: Antarctic sea ice hits fourth-straight near-record low
items.what: Antarctica's winter sea ice peaked at 17.59 million square kilometres this year, likely the third-lowest on record and about 6% below the 1981–2010 average. It's the fourth year running that Antarctic ice has ranked among the four lowest ever measured.
items.why_it_matters: Less sea ice means less sunlight reflected back to space, which can accelerate warming and disrupt weather patterns far beyond Antarctica.
items.context: Sea ice around Antarctica grows each winter and shrinks each summer; scientists track its yearly peak to spot long-term trends. Four record-low years in a row is unusual for a region once thought more stable than the Arctic.
items.next: Scientists will watch whether this summer's melt sets an outright record low.

items.headline: Hundreds of hidden 'iceberg quakes' found at Thwaites Glacier
items.what: Scientists catalogued 362 previously uncounted seismic events, including 245 near Thwaites Glacier's ocean edge, caused mostly by huge icebergs breaking off, capsizing and colliding with the ice. Activity peaked between 2018 and 2020, when the glacier was flowing fastest toward the sea.
items.why_it_matters: The quake pattern lining up with the glacier's fastest movement gives scientists a new tool to track how quickly it's destabilising.
items.context: Thwaites, nicknamed the 'Doomsday Glacier,' is roughly the size of Florida, and scientists fear its collapse alone could eventually raise global sea levels by over half a metre.
items.next: Researchers will look for the same signal at other fast-melting glaciers using this improved detection method.

items.headline: NASA's Curiosity rover marks 5,000 days on Mars
items.what: Curiosity has now logged 5,000 Martian days — over 14 Earth years — since landing in Gale Crater in 2012, far outliving its planned two-year mission. NASA marked the milestone with new panoramic images from the rover's current spot near Mount Sharp.
items.why_it_matters: Curiosity's longevity keeps yielding fresh clues about whether Mars could once have supported life, well beyond what its designers expected.
items.context: A Martian day, or 'sol,' is about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day. Curiosity has recently found the most diverse mix of carbon-based organic molecules yet seen on Mars.
items.next: NASA continues driving Curiosity up the slopes of Mount Sharp toward new rock layers.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: Kimi Antonelli closed in on a record-breaking Mercedes title, while Red Bull's winless 2026 season continued.

items.headline: Kimi Antonelli closes in on record-breaking F1 title
items.what: Mercedes rookie Kimi Antonelli leads the 2026 F1 championship by 81 points over teammate George Russell, with eight rounds left. At 20, he's on track to become Formula 1's youngest-ever world champion.
items.why_it_matters: A 20-year-old title winner would be a changing-of-the-guard moment for F1, and raises questions about how Mercedes manages two internal rivals.
items.context: Mercedes has fielded two title contenders this year, an unusual situation in F1's team-orders-sensitive culture. Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and McLaren's Lando Norris trail further behind, both over 100 points back.
items.next: Watch for any team-order tension as Mercedes balances both drivers' title hopes over the final rounds.
items.insight: Mercedes running two genuine title contenders is a gamble — team orders now would spark fan backlash, but letting them race freely risks costing Mercedes the constructors' title too.

items.headline: Verstappen, Red Bull still winless through most of 2026
items.what: Max Verstappen finished behind George Russell at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, extending Red Bull's winless run deep into the season. Four-time champion Verstappen remains mathematically alive but far off the Mercedes duo's pace at the front.
items.why_it_matters: A season without a single Red Bull win would mark the end of the team's era of dominance, at least for now.
items.context: Verstappen won four consecutive drivers' titles from 2021 to 2024, making Red Bull's current form one of the biggest reversals in recent F1 history.
items.next: Watch whether Red Bull can find late-season form, or whether focus shifts fully to 2027's car rules.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: Pakistan's cricket crisis deepened with a new inquiry, while West Indies' Campbell smashed a record century against India.

items.headline: Pakistan cricket launches new probe amid crisis
items.what: The Pakistan Cricket Board has opened an internal disciplinary inquiry into the team's conduct, days after axing seven players and two coaches following a 3-0 Test whitewash in England — the country's worst-ever result on English soil.
items.why_it_matters: The instability threatens Pakistan's preparation for upcoming series, and raises real questions about whether the current setup can rebuild the team.
items.context: Pakistan cricket has churned through six head coaches in two years and three board chairmen since 2023, a chaos former captain Shahid Afridi called unprecedented.
items.next: Watch for the inquiry's findings and whether more players or staff face action.
items.insight: Constant coaching and board turnover, not just results, may be the deeper problem — a team can't build a settled game plan under six coaches in two years.

items.headline: West Indies batter smashes fastest ODI ton vs India
items.what: West Indies opener John Campbell scored 101 off just 68 balls in the second ODI at Guwahati, the fastest ODI century by a West Indies batter against India. West Indies posted 403/7 after India chose to field first.
items.why_it_matters: A record-breaking innings against a strong Indian bowling attack is a statement West Indies cricket, often written off, can still produce match-winners.
items.context: India, led by Shubman Gill after Rohit Sharma's reduced ODI role, is playing a three-match series against the West Indies at home.
items.next: Watch whether India can chase down West Indies' total and level the series.

watch_tomorrow: RBI's rate decision looms October 5-7 amid a split on hiking.
Morocco's Mansouri must form a coalition government in the coming weeks.
Supreme Court reviews CPCB's barium-firecracker report by October 15.
Watch for oil-price moves on any fresh Hormuz diplomatic signal.
India, West Indies play the series decider after Guwahati's high-scoring ODI.
